posts.author: HoloM
posts.content_md:
Today I made a H2 copy of a laserstransmissionhologram: 

![Image](http://4c-s.org/v-web/gallery/albums/album16/dragon.jpg)

What I don't understand, is the color of the hologram. I used PFG-01 pretreated with 2% TEA. So the image should be between yellow and green. 

It's indeed in the green, but what I have never seen on a H2 is, that it's not sharp because the colors are not really monochromatic. You see a smear of colors on the edges of the object, I have seen this in DCGs but not with silver halide. Please explain, what's the reason and how to avoid? 

Thanks

Matthias

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
The color smear has to do with the processing. What processing did you use?

Also in high humidity holos will not achieve their final color for a few days.

posts.author: HoloM
posts.content_md: Colin, are you sure? I use ascorbate developer and edta bleach. if it would be a matter of processing, i would have this effect in denisyuks, too, don't I?. the object smears in rainbow colors, like in achromatic holograms, or often seen in DCG. I don't believe it's the processing, could it have something to do with angle or distance of reference beam? the effect is nearly like if you view a lasertransmisionhologram in white light, but not so strong. And I think the effect is more worse the more the object is away from the film plane. In the film plane this effect is nearly not visible.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
The farther you go from the film plane the more chromatic aberation there will be in any reflection hologram. The only way to avoid this is to have a narrower replay. Tom B. posted something a little while ago that he thinks the size of the film makes a difference. An interesting thought I have not had time to mull over. (Perhaps field of view makes a difference?)

I bet if you search the forum for silver and broadband together you will find a thread I was invloved in in trying to make single beam holograms more broadband.

I am not sure why you would have more of a problem with H2s than single beams unless the exposure energy was different.

And I think the effect is more worse the more the object is away from the film plane. In the film plane this effect is nearly not visible.

Hi Matthias.

I can go as far as telling you that this effect is caused by what is described in Graham Saxby’s “Practical Holography” as ‘chirped fringes”

which means the fringe widths on the top surface differ from those lower down. The standard reply to explaining the cause is as Colin indicated…. processing technique. 

But in your case I would hazard a guess that it may be more unusual.

as you indicate yourself.

I think you may actually have got your H2 object beam too strong (!) compared to the reference beam. You may have got “overmodulation” . 

jeff

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md: I've had the same thing happen to me as Jeff describes. When the object light is very much brighter than the reference light. Check your light ratios. I'm betting you got them backwards so that the ref beam is much weaker than the object light.
